text.text: Evidence on the associations between social media use (SMU) and youth affect remains inconsistent, partly because it remains unclear how active versus passive engagement differs in daily life, whether these relationships are bidirectional, and how individual characteristics such as gender and mental health symptoms moderate them.

We utilized ecological momentary assessment (EMA) via a smartphone app to sample real-world affect and SMU (active [posting/messaging] vs. passive [browsing]) among 80 young people (Mean age=20.1 years) with varying depression and anhedonia, yielding 2,316 observations across six consecutive days.
Multilevel regressions revealed that, concurrently, SMU was associated with lower positive affect (PA; β=-0.35, p<.001) and higher negative affect (NA; β=0.22, p=.002).
text.formatted: Multilevel regressions revealed that, concurrently, SMU was associated with lower positive affect (PA; β=-0.35, p<.001) and higher negative affect (NA; β=0.22, p=.002).

text.text: Crucially, this negative affect association was weaker among individuals with higher depression (β=-0.02, p=.04) but stronger among those with higher anhedonia (β=0.04, p=.02).

Conversely, active (vs. passive) use was concurrently linked to higher PA (β=4.12, p<.001) and lower NA (β=-2.01, p=.05), with these favourable associations stronger among males than females and among individuals with lower depression symptoms (β=0.06, p=.03).
text.formatted: Conversely, active (vs. passive) use was concurrently linked to higher PA (β=4.12, p<.001) and lower NA (β=-2.01, p=.05), with these favourable associations stronger among males than females and among individuals with lower depression symptoms (β=0.06, p=.03).

text.text: In time-lagged analyses, higher PA predicted a lower subsequent likelihood of active versus passive use (β=-1.23, p=.01), while SMU itself did not predict subsequent affect.
These findings emphasize that while general SMU coincides with less favourable affect, active engagement might offer situational benefits over passive browsing.

Crucially, these dynamic relationships depend heavily on gender and distinct psychological vulnerabilities, demonstrating the necessity of distinguishing depression from anhedonia in digital mental health research.
>Introduction

text.text: Social media use (SMU) has become an integral daily-life component for most adolescents and young adults, who use it for establishing and maintaining social connections, information-seeking, inspiration, and entertainment (van der Wal et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Social media use (SMU) has become an integral daily-life component for most adolescents and young adults, who use it for establishing and maintaining social connections, information-seeking, inspiration, and entertainment <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(van der Wal et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Recent findings suggest that 32% of adolescents meet the criteria of intensive or problematic SMU (World Health Organization, 2024).
text.formatted: Recent findings suggest that 32% of adolescents meet the criteria of intensive or problematic SMU <ref type="bibr">(World Health Organization, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, population-level investigation has highlighted that more than half of adolescents, who use at least one social media platform, report an average usage of more than four hours per day (McAlister et al., 2024).

text.text: Given the widespread adoption and intensive engagement with social media among young people, considerable research has sought to understand its potential effects on mental health and wellbeing, but the findings are inconsistent.

Evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses indicates that problematic SMU is associated with a range of adverse mental health outcomes, including depression, anxiety, stress, and loneliness (Huang, 2022; Shannon et al., 2022; Ulvi et al., 2022).

text.text: Conversely other studies find that social media use may confer benefits, including facilitating social connectedness, enabling authentic self-expression, and reducing stress (Grieve & Watkinson, 2016; Karim et al., 2020; Reinecke & Trepte, 2014; Ulvi et al., 2022), and other studies report no relationships between social media use and mental health outcomes (Berryman et al., 2018; Coyne et al., 2020).

text.text: One reason for inconsistencies across studies could be that the relationship between SMU and mental health depends on how SMU is being used.

Recent research has categorised social media use into active (e.g., messaging, posting, commenting) and passive (e.g., browsing, scrolling) forms, with passive use hypothesised to be more detrimental to mental health than active use (Valkenburg, van Driel, et al., 2021).

text.text: Consistent with this view, some studies have found that greater passive use is associated with higher levels of depression and anxiety in both retrospective (Thorisdottir et al., 2019) and real-time assessments (Nereim et al., 2020).

text.text: However, other studies have failed to replicate these findings (Smout et al., 2026; Valkenburg, Beyens, et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020).

text.text: Consequently, it remains unclear whether active forms of social media use, such as messaging and posting, are more beneficial for mental health and wellbeing than passive activities, such as scrolling and browsing.
Individual differences in internalising symptoms, such as depression and anxiety may also confer susceptibility to the negative effects of social media use (Beyens et al., 2020).

text.text: Gender may also moderate these associations, as studies show social media use is associated with lower well-being and higher levels of depression symptoms in females than in males (Kelly et al., 2018; Twenge & Martin, 2020).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that the relationship between social media use and wellbeing may vary according to individual characteristics.

However, most studies to date have not yet examined how individual characteristics influence the outcomes of social media use, therefore further research is needed to determine how factors such as gender and mental health status moderate the associations between social media use and affective wellbeing in daily life.
Momentary affective states, including positive affect (PA) and negative affect (NA), may be particularly sensitive to the effects of social media use (Dienlin & Johannes, 2020).

text.text: For example, studies that assessed the experimental effect of social media use upon affective states in college students found that PA decreased by approximately 20% following social media use (Lepp & Barkley, 2022), and depressive symptoms were associated with students feeling worse (increased NA or decreased PA) (Tuck et al., 2025).

text.text: The inconsistencies in these findings might be attributed to different study designs.

Experimental studies establish causality but rely on researcher-imposed exposure that might not fully reflect real-life situations, while cross-sectional and conventional longitudinal designs typically rely on retrospective self-reports or widely spaced assessments (e.g., weeks or months), which are less sensitive to momentary changes and more susceptible to recall bias.

These limitations can be addressed by Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) via repeatedly sampling participants' experiences and behaviour within their natural environment multiple times a day for several days usually via a smartphone device, enabling the capture of moment-to-moment temporal dynamics while reducing recall bias and enhancing ecological validity (Shiffman et al., 2008).

text.text: EMA studies have begun to reveal complex bidirectional associations between social media use and affect.

For example, negative perceptions of social media chatting predicted subsequent increases in negative affect (NA), while higher NA also predicted more negative perceptions of chatting, although this reverse association was weaker (Brimmel et al., 2025).

text.text: Furthermore, Politte-Corn et al. (2024) found that social media use predicted both immediate and subsequent decreases in PA among adolescents with and without depression, while also predicting subsequent decreases in NA among adolescents with depression.

text.text: Collectively, these findings highlight the value of EMA for investigating the dynamic relationship between social media use and affect in daily life.

Nevertheless, evidence remains limited regarding how specific patterns of social media use, particularly active versus passive use, relate to momentary affect and whether these associations differ according to individual characteristics, such as gender and depression.

Although individual characteristics may explain some of the heterogeneity in findings, it remains unclear how mental health symptoms and gender moderate the relationship between social media use (SMU) and affect.

Depression is among the most extensively studied mental health conditions in this context and is often operationalised primarily in terms of low mood, one of the two core symptoms of Major Depressive Disorder (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
However, considerably less attention has been paid to the other core symptom, anhedonia.

Characterised by diminished interest and pleasure, anhedonia is closely linked to positive affect and reward processing (Kaya & McCabe, 2019; Ma et al., 2026; McCabe, 2018; Rizvi et al., 2016), and may therefore influence affective experiences during social media use by altering the extent to which its rewarding aspects are experienced.
text.formatted: Characterised by diminished interest and pleasure, anhedonia is closely linked to positive affect and reward processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kaya & McCabe, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Ma et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">McCabe, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Rizvi et al., 2016)</ref>, and may therefore influence affective experiences during social media use by altering the extent to which its rewarding aspects are experienced.

text.text: EMA studies suggest that individuals with higher anhedonia engage more passively with social media (Zhan & Wang, 2026) and anticipate less pleasure from checking social media, although their experienced pleasure during use may not differ (Dreier et al., 2026).
text.formatted: EMA studies suggest that individuals with higher anhedonia engage more passively with social media <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Zhan & Wang, 2026)</ref> and anticipate less pleasure from checking social media, although their experienced pleasure during use may not differ <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dreier et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Depression and anhedonia may therefore be associated with distinct patterns of affect during social media use.
For example, people with higher depression symptoms may already experience elevated negative affect, potentially limiting the additional increase associated with social media use.
In contrast, people with higher anhedonia may experience less reward from social media engagement, potentially contributing to less favourable affective experiences.

These possibilities remain tentative, and to our knowledge no study has examined whether depression and anhedonia moderate the momentary associations between social media use and affect in daily life.

Therefore, the present study used ecological momentary assessment (EMA) to examine concurrent and time-lagged associations between momentary positive and negative affect and social media use in young people.
We distinguished social media use from non-use and, among assessments involving social media use, active engagement (posting or messaging) from passive engagement (browsing).
We also examined whether these associations varied according to gender, depression symptoms and anhedonia.

By considering depression and anhedonia separately, the study aimed to clarify whether the affective correlates of social media use differ according to engagement type and individual psychological characteristics.
Finally, we examined whether affect predicted subsequent social media engagement and whether social media use predicted subsequent affect.

After this, participants proceeded to indicate whether their next activity would be using social media and their future usage patterns.

Participants were then required to log on and fill in their age, gender, ethnicity, the MFQ, and the ASA.

Participants were asked to respond to each assessment as soon as possible; otherwise, it would expire.

text.text: Therefore, these variables were also added as covariates in models predicting their respective outcomes.
Next, we ran multilevel models with SMU and active/passive use as predictors of PA and NA, respectively.
We applied an iterative model build-up strategy to test the interactive effects of SMU and active/passive use with, depression, anhedonia and gender on momentary PA and NA.

For each outcome (PA and NA), in step 1 we introduced fixed effects of level 1 predictors SMU and active/passive use separately, and we introduced fixed effects of the time-invariant level 3 predictors (depression, anhedonia and gender).
In step 2, we examined the moderating effects of the time-invariant predictors by adding cross-level interactions between level 1 predictors (SMU and active/passive use) and level 3 predictors.
We also investigated the bidirectional temporal predictions between affect, SMU, and active/passive use using time-lagged analyses.

To examine whether SMU and active/passive use predicted PA and NA at next assessment, we modelled PA and NA as outcomes at (t) using multilevel linear models with SMU and active/passive use separately as predictors at (t-1).

Similarly, to examine whether affect predicted SMU and active/passive use at next assessment, we modelled SMU and active/passive use at (t) using multilevel logistic models with PA and NA as predictors at (t-1).

We also applied the iterative model build-up strategy to these models, introducing only fixed effects in step 1 and cross-level interactions in step 2 to examine the moderating effects of the time-invariant predictors (depression, anhedonia and gender).

This study examined how social media use and active versus passive engagement were associated with momentary affect in young people, and whether these associations varied according to depression symptoms, anhedonia and gender.
Three findings are particularly noteworthy.
First, social media use was concurrently associated with lower positive affect and higher negative affect, whereas active engagement was associated with more favourable affect than passive browsing.

Second, the association between social media use and negative affect varied in opposite directions according to depression and anhedonia symptoms: it was weaker among participants with higher depression symptoms but stronger among those with higher anhedonia.
Third, higher positive affect predicted a lower likelihood of active relative to passive engagement at the subsequent assessment, although social media use did not predict subsequent affect.

Together, these findings suggest that the concurrent association between social media use and affect depends on both engagement type and individual psychological characteristics, while providing limited evidence about temporal directionality.

We found that SMU was associated with decreased momentary PA and increased NA in young people, consistent with most previous EMA (Hamilton et al., 2021; Politte-Corn et al., 2024) and non-EMA findings (Tuck et al., 2025).

This finding adds to the limited real-life EMA evidence (Nereim et al., 2020) and retrospective findings (Thorisdottir et al., 2019).

text.text: However, these observational associations do not establish that active use improves affect.
They could also reflect the type of interaction, the situations in which young people choose to engage actively, or pre-existing differences in affect.

A particularly important finding was that depression and anhedonia moderated the association between social media use and negative affect in opposite directions, despite both being core features of depressive symptomatology.
Consistent with Politte-Corn et al.
(2024), this association was weaker among participants with higher depression symptoms, whereas it was stronger among those with higher anhedonia.
As Figure 1 shows, participants with higher depression symptoms reported elevated negative affect regardless of social media use.

text.text: The weaker association may therefore reflect this already elevated level of negative affect, leaving less room for a further increase during social media use.

An alternative or complementary explanation is emotion context insensitivity (ECI), whereby depression is associated with blunted emotional reactivity to both positive and negative stimuli (Bylsma et al., 2011; Rottenberg et al., 2005).

text.text: The present data cannot distinguish these explanations.

In contrast, the stronger association among participants with higher anhedonia suggests that anhedonia may be relevant not only to how young people engage with social media, but also to their momentary affect during use.
One possibility is that individuals experiencing reduced interest and pleasure derive less reward from their social media experiences, potentially contributing to less favourable affect.
However, because the study did not directly measure the rewarding qualities of social media content or participants' motives for using it, this interpretation remains tentative.
These contrasting associations highlight the value of examining depression and anhedonia separately rather than treating depressive symptomatology as a unitary construct.
To our knowledge, this is the first study to show that depression and gender also moderate the association between active (vs. passive) SMU and affect.

Consistent with the ECI account, individuals with higher depression may derive fewer affective benefits from active engagement due to reduced reward responsiveness (Berry et al., 2019; Foti & Hajcak, 2009; Halahakoon et al., 2020).

text.text: Therefore, young females may experience more mixed emotional outcomes from active SMU, while young males derive more consistent affective benefits.
This moderating effect of gender was not observed in all prior studies (Politte-Corn et al., 2024), highlighting the need for further research on how gender shapes the affective correlates of SMU.

text.text: This study also examined time-lagged associations between affect and active versus passive social media use.
Higher positive affect predicted a lower likelihood of active (rather than passive) use at the subsequent assessment.
However, social media use did not predict subsequent positive or negative affect, and some time-lagged interaction models did not converge.

The single prospective association should therefore be interpreted cautiously: it does not establish why participants were less likely to engage actively after reporting higher positive affect, and it provides limited evidence for a general mood-regulation account.
Further research with more frequent observations and larger numbers of social media use assessments is needed to clarify the temporal relationship between affect and engagement type.
This study has several limitations.

Social media use was recorded when it was the main current activity, which likely underestimated use and yielded relatively few social media use assessments (121 in total, including 32 active-use assessments).
Estimates involving active versus passive use, particularly the moderation effects, should therefore be interpreted cautiously and replicated in larger samples.
The sample was also small and included relatively few male participants, so gender differences require replication in larger, more gender-balanced samples.

Some time-lagged interaction models did not converge, and analyses were not corrected for multiple comparisons; moderation findings, particularly those with p values close to .05, should be considered provisional.
Future studies combining EMA with passive sensing of smartphone and app use could provide more precise measures of social media engagement.
Overall, this study suggests that the association between social media use and momentary affect in young people is not uniform.
Social media use was associated with lower positive and higher negative affect, while active engagement was associated with more favourable affect than passive browsing.

Crucially, the association between social media use and negative affect was stronger at higher levels of anhedonia but weaker at higher levels of depression symptoms; the latter pattern may reflect the already elevated negative affect reported by participants with higher depression.
Higher positive affect also predicted a lower likelihood of subsequent active relative to passive engagement, although social media use did not predict subsequent affect.
These findings highlight the importance of considering both engagement type and individual psychological characteristics, particularly the distinction between depression and anhedonia.

Given the observational design, relatively few social media use assessments and multiple exploratory moderation analyses, replication in larger samples is needed before drawing firm conclusions about the mechanisms underlying these associations or their implications for intervention.
